name: Betel chewing

card.summary: The traditional Asian and Pacific habit of chewing areca nut with betel leaf and lime, which produces a warm, alert feeling and, with long use, red-stained teeth and gums.
card.aka: Paan, betel quid chewing, areca nut chewing
card.note: Linked by cancer researchers to oral submucous fibrosis and oral and oesophageal cancer; tobacco added to the quid raises the risk further.

quick.overview:
Betel chewing means holding a quid of areca nut, slaked lime and betel leaf in the mouth, often with flavourings, and spitting out the juice. It is a long-standing social and ceremonial custom in South and Southeast Asia, Micronesia and Melanesia, and in diaspora communities. Its effect on appearance is a visible one: saliva turns red and long-term chewers develop stained teeth and gums, and chewing is reported to cause facial flushing and a warm feeling.

Most people who chew do so for the stimulation or for social and ritual reasons, not for looks. Research has examined its effects on the nervous system and heart rate and, extensively, its link to oral disease. Dental and cancer researchers report staining, oral submucous fibrosis and increased oral cancer risk.
quick.how: People chew a prepared quid, commonly sold as paan, and spit rather than swallow it. Recipes vary by region and may add spices, sweeteners or tobacco. It is offered to guests, used at weddings and festivals, and chewed through the day by regular users. Staining builds up with long use.
quick.risks: The International Agency for Research on Cancer and many reviews link betel quid to oral and oesophageal cancer, and oral submucous fibrosis, a scarring condition that can limit mouth opening. Tobacco added to the quid raises risk further, and chewing during pregnancy is linked to adverse outcomes. Several places, including Dubai and parts of Myanmar, restrict sale or use.

lead: Betel chewing, also called betel quid or areca nut chewing, is the practice of chewing areca nut, slaked lime and betel (Piper betle) leaf, sometimes with spices, sweeteners or tobacco, for a mild stimulant effect. Wikipedia estimates about 600 million regular users worldwide [1].

Its relevance to appearance is mainly visible effects: chewing produces profuse red saliva and, after long use, lasting red staining of the teeth [1]. Clinical reviews of oral submucous fibrosis list blanching of oral mucosa and staining of teeth and gingiva among its signs [2]. In a small clinical study, chewers' ear temperature rose by about 2 degrees C, matching the facial flush and warmth users describe [3]. The habit is also a cultural symbol: paan is offered as hospitality and used in weddings, festivals and worship, and betel kits have served as royal regalia and wedding gifts [1].

A large research literature, including a 2015 meta-analysis, links betel quid, even without tobacco, to oral cancer and precancer [4]. People sometimes confuse its stains with the deliberate tooth blackening practised historically in parts of Asia, a separate custom.

angle.text: Betel chewing is mainly a social, ritual and stimulant habit, and its effect on looks is a by-product: red saliva and, with long use, stained teeth and gums. It is documented here because of that visible effect and its associated oral health risks.

paras: A betel quid is built from areca nut, slaked lime and betel leaf. Regional versions add coconut, dates, sugar, menthol, saffron, clove, aniseed or cardamom, and tobacco may be added or may replace the nut [1]. The mixture is chewed and the juice is spat out [1]. Users report a warm, alert feeling, and studies describe sweating, salivation, faster heart rate and a sense of well-being associated with the alkaloid arecoline [5][6].

Arecoline traces have been found in the teeth of foragers on Sulawesi dating to roughly 25,000 to 6,300 years ago, and the oldest evidence of betel with lime comes from a Philippine cave dated to about 4,600 years ago [1]. The habit spread with Austronesian migration to Micronesia, South India, Sri Lanka and later Madagascar [1]. Antonio Pigafetta described chewing in the Philippines in 1521, and a 16th-century Indian cookbook shows a sultan preparing paan [1].

In South Asia paan is a gesture of hospitality and appears at weddings; in Vietnam betel and areca symbolise marriage, and in Malaysia betel kits were royal regalia [1]. A survey of Taiwan found the habit common among both ethnic Chinese and Indigenous residents [7].

sections.h: Effects on appearance and oral health
paras: Chewing stains saliva red and, with years of use, teeth permanently; spit stains on streets are also a public nuisance in some cities [1]. Oral submucous fibrosis, a premalignant condition attributed to betel chewing, presents with blanched mucosa, stained teeth and gums and trismus (limited mouth opening) [2]. Reviews implicate arecoline and copper in the condition [2].

A 1989 review described the cytotoxic and mutagenic potential of quid ingredients and the formation of nitrosation products [8]. A meta-analysis found that betel quid without tobacco is associated with oral cancer and precancer [4]. A Taiwanese case-control study reported 3.6-fold and 9.2-fold oesophageal cancer risk at moderate and heavy cumulative chewing, respectively [9]. Reviews of smokeless tobacco report that betel chewing, with or without tobacco, can lead to oral premalignant lesions [10]. Wikipedia reports the IARC has reviewed betel quid and areca nut chewing and notes adverse pregnancy outcomes, while a 1924 BMJ item shows the cancer association has been discussed for a century [1][11].
Neuroscience studies describe heart-rate and skin-temperature effects, and arecoline-linked habituation and withdrawal in chewers [3][5][6].
Yangon banned betel in 1995, betel chewing was banned at Shwedagon Pagoda in 2007, and Dubai banned import and sale of betel quid in 2008; many places have anti-spitting laws [1].

Human studies are mostly epidemiological and physiological. A controlled clinical study found chewing raised ear and forehead skin temperature, an effect largely abolished by atropine [3]. Doppler and sympathetic-response studies recorded cerebral blood-flow and autonomic effects [5][12]. Epidemiological work links chewing to oral submucous fibrosis, oral leukoplakia and cancer, and to oesophageal cancer [4][9][13].
